title: Compact signed-state arithmetic (V6)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Can a small model solve short accounting stories when transfers are given as signed changes to entity balances?
settings: 88,430 parameters, 19 compact positions
data: synthetic accounting stories
results: 95.50% answer accuracy (historical record; checkpoint selection reused the reported test split)
lesson: Arithmetic stories become easier once identity, direction, amount and operation are explicit; this did not show open-language understanding.

title: Canonicalization and decomposition (Phase 7)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Can the arithmetic core generalise beyond the names and items seen in training?
settings: frozen V6 core plus deterministic front end
data: 5,000 examples with new names and items
results: retraining with explicit slots: 27.64% answer, 13.83% state accuracy
deterministic front end (canonical identities, item selection, signed deltas): 95.24% on 5,000 examples
cross-item composition without retraining: 94.62% over 5,000 examples
lesson: The first compiler result: a deterministic front end normalised surface variation, but reliability then depended on the compiler.

title: Orchestration, relations and specialist composition (Phases 8-10)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Can compiler transformations add operations around a fixed core, and can relation specialists be composed with it?
settings: message-passing relation model 19,351 parameters; composed system 107,781 parameters
data: synthetic snapshot/cancellation/time/conditional queries; multi-hop ordering; 5,000 cross-domain queries
results: snapshot 99.58%, cancellation 99.56%, between-time 99.34%, conditional 99.64%
generic compact Transformer on multi-hop ordering: 65.57% entity distance, 18.56% exact world
message passing: 100% entity distance, reachability and exact world; vectorised version about 2.79x faster
Phase 10 composed specialists: 94.74% on 5,000 cross-domain queries
lesson: Architecture matched to the task operation worked, but representation and architecture changed together, so compactness alone was not isolated.

title: Dynamic graphs, references, streaming and composed programs (Phases 11-12)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Does the approach hold as state and control per problem grow?
settings: not recorded
data: synthetic dynamic graphs, event references, large-world streams; 5,000 composed query programs
results: dynamic state-dependent graphs 97.68%
event references 93.64%
recursive large-world streaming: query accuracy 19.3%, 14.3%, 13.6% at 8, 16, 32 entities
held-out composed query programs: 98.02% across 5,000 examples
lesson: A fixed-size recurrent state can accept longer input without keeping the distinctions needed; executable length is not reasoning quality.

title: Query VM and the parsing pivot (Phase 13)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: How much of the high accuracy comes from parsing language correctly?
settings: not recorded
data: 6,000 supported paraphrases
results: VM variants: raw 91.30%, invariant candidates 93.07%, four-permutation verification 93.55%, adaptive 93.43%
learned byte-level convolutional parser: 36.52% exact parse, 51.28% end-answer accuracy
deterministic controlled-language parser: 100% exact parse, 99.13% answers
lesson: Much of the earlier accuracy came from correct parsing; text-to-structure learning was the unresolved problem.

title: Workflow prediction against subword controls (Phases 14-17)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Does a compact typed representation beat a subword control on a hidden-rule workflow task?
settings: compact 72,835 params / 21 positions vs subword 78,083 params / 193 positions (Phase 14); hierarchy about 73K vs control about 62K (Phase 17)
data: synthetic workflow tasks; Phase 17 majority-class raw baseline 83.67%
results: Phase 14: 72.89% vs 71.55% balanced accuracy; 0.25 ms vs 0.666 ms model latency
Phase 15: IID 74.84% vs 66.83%; risk-prior shift 66.95% vs 67.71% (control ahead); alias 75.80% vs 33.33% (inputs not equivalent)
Phase 16 hierarchical 73,219 params on 60-event inputs: 81.40% raw, 61.88% balanced
Phase 17: compact 83.83% raw / 63.85% balanced / macro F1 0.611 / 0.647 ms vs control 79.63% / 62.02% / 0.569 / 2.152 ms
lesson: A small efficiency edge on synthetic workflows, with confounds (unequal inputs, more parameters); no broad advantage follows.

title: Multi-incident routing and fixed-capacity memory (Phases 18-30)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Can routing, dual streams, recurrent memory, adapters and planning handle target incidents among distractors and long event streams?
settings: dual-stream 144,292 params; recurrent 72,382 params
data: synthetic multi-incident workflows, 160-640 events
results: structured multi-incident 66.82% raw, 61.39% balanced
dual-stream 65.33% raw, 61.25% balanced vs 56.54% streaming baseline
selective structured model 95% answered-case accuracy at about 24% coverage
recurrent: balanced 57.26% at 160 events, about 50-52% at 320, 42-47% at 640
new-policy adapters plateau 47-49%; explanation prediction about 25%; planner 3.1% exact vs 4.8% oracle, regret about 2.82
lesson: A fixed-size state can process a long sequence without retaining the relevant detail; more width or routing did not guarantee better decisions.

title: Semantic V1: text to typed events (V1 Experimental)
phase: 1 · Where it started: September research
question: Can a learned parser reliably bind visible language to an explicit typed program?
settings: lexical attachment parser 919,045 params, width 192, two local and two reasoning layers, 91 vocabulary entries, 4 entities, 24 clauses, 160 positions per clause; learned core 346 params; preservation recipe 1,500 updates, freeze after update 300 (909,072 protected), 9,973 role parameters trained
data: synthetic accounting and relation worlds; 400 development worlds per seed (200 per task)
results: early raw text-to-answer paths near 31%; structured inputs 100% on IID tasks
routine regression: 100% complete programs and both answer paths on all three seeds
seeds 419 and 383 passed all observed development gates; seed 433 failed: 76% accounting program accuracy on unfamiliar wording, 38% on the combined shift
108 automated tests pass; reserved final evaluation not run
lesson: Explicit semantics make a small specialist precise inside its contract; correct answers can hide wrong internal roles, and text-to-structure generalisation remains the bottleneck.

title: Compiler v0 initial measurements
phase: 2 · A compiler between language and the model
question: Does a stateless single-pass dictionary encoder match BPE on sequence length and learnable structure?
settings: dictionaries 8k-64k with/without case flags and phrases; Witten-Bell n-gram orders 1-3 as proxy; C++ speed best of 5 on 2 cores
data: 48 training books, 45.0 MB; held-out 1.06 MB (3 books); repository Markdown and Python as out-of-domain
results: bytes: 1000 IDs/KB, n-gram 2.893 bits/byte
in-house BPE 32k: 253.9 IDs/KB, 1.866
v0 32k plain: 254.3 IDs/KB, 1.865; encode 112.5 MB/s, decode 301.4 MB/s (Python reference 4.4 MB/s)
v0 32k plain + 4k phrases: 185.2 IDs/KB, 1.921; v0 64k + 8k phrases: 169.8, 1.946
case flags cost 6% longer sequences for no proxy gain
19 contract tests pass; C++ matches Python byte for byte
lesson: Plain v0 matches an in-house BPE on the proxy; phrases shorten sequences 27-33% for a 3-4% worse proxy, a question left for neural tests.
sources: docs/ENCODER_RESEARCH_PLAN.md: Appendix A, sections 1 and 2.3 F4

title: Repository review: encoder weaknesses F1-F9
phase: 2 · A compiler between language and the model
question: What distortions in corpus and encoder must be fixed before neural tests?
settings: not recorded
data: Heart of Darkness (211 KB UTF-8) and The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (563 KB) held-out books
results: F1: bare words 11.9% and 11.6% of words, about two thirds line-initial; newline units 6.0% and 7.2% of units
F2: ASCII punctuation 16.4-16.5% of units; runs as one unit would save 2.3-2.4% of IDs
F3: UTF-8 punctuation 1.3% of units in Heart of Darkness (684 byte IDs for 228 characters)
F7: 45 MB is about 11.4M v0 IDs, too small for a 25M model
F9: dictionaries fitted on novels need 231-278 IDs/KB on Markdown and 317-375 on Python vs 170-254 on books
verdict: fixes planned (paragraph unwrapping later used in the cleaned mixes)
lesson: Hard-wrapped Gutenberg text and byte-level punctuation distort a books-only dictionary; the dictionary must match the text the model will see.

title: Phase 1 model-shape calibration on CPU
phase: 2 · A compiler between language and the model
question: How long does a training step take for byte and 32k-vocabulary models on the sandbox CPU?
settings: random IDs, batch 8, context 256, AdamW, fp32, CPU 4 threads, mean of 6 steps after warm-up
data: not recorded
results: bytes, width 128, 4 layers: 0.79M non-embedding, 0.19 s/step, 11,000 IDs/s
v0 32k, width 128: 5.02M total, 1.46 s/step, 1,400 IDs/s
v0 32k, width 256: 11.61M total, 3.89 s/step, 530 IDs/s
embedding and tied 32k output layer about 87% of the step at width 128
verdict: adopted (budget in IDs processed; factorised output moved up)
lesson: At small width the output layer dominates cost, so a large vocabulary costs more per pass than bytes despite shorter sequences.

title: Ladder 1: six encodings at equal time
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Does compiled text beat raw bytes, phrases and a dictionary-free hash encoder, and do tables help?
settings: 4 layers, width 128, context 256, batch 16, 600 s each on a 4-core CPU, seed 1
data: 45 MB books corpus (48 books); held-out three books; OOD repository Markdown and Python
results: held-out bits/byte: bytes 2.181, v0 8k 2.007, phrases <=3 2.057, phrases <=6 2.075, hash 4096x4096 2.037, v0 8k + 2^20 bigram table (136.09M params) 1.939
talk-back bytes/s: bytes 293, v0 8k 732, table 848, hash 589 (after mask fix; 258 in the ladder run)
equal text (15.1 MB): bytes 2.232, v0 8k 2.109, hash 2.099, table 2.030
hash fidelity 98.70% / 98.41% / 95.67%; 508 units lost to collisions (0.02% of occurrences)
hash re-run 2.034 vs 2.037 (0.2%, first noise measure)
verdict: adopted: compiled words + tables; phrase IDs rejected as a sequence device
lesson: Compiling text beat bytes by 8% at equal compute and talked back 2.5x faster; phrases cut length 18% but were 2.5-3.4% worse because phrase codes are rarer and hide their words.

title: Ladder 2a: hashed table scaling
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: How far do hashed n-gram input tables scale on the same core?
settings: v0 8k, width 128 core, 600 s, seed 1; bigram tables 2^18/2^20/2^22 rows, bigram+trigram 2^20 each
data: 45 MB books corpus
results: steps/s drop 5-13%; talk-back unchanged within noise
run-to-run speed noise about +-8%
a configuration-name bug crashed ladder 2a at launch and cost an hour (watcher did not notice); fixed
lesson: Every table helps 3.4-4.7% at small cost, but rows scale weakly at 45 MB; a trigram order beat quadrupling rows.

title: Ladder 2b screen: do tables stack on other encoders?
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Do bigram+trigram tables help the hash encoder and raw bytes as well as words?
settings: 4-minute runs, 2^20 rows each table, width 128
data: 45 MB books corpus
results: bytes about 2.49 -> 2.314 (about 7%; byte baseline read off ladder 1 curve)
bytes + tables still 5.7% behind plain words without tables
lesson: Tables help most where units carry least, but do not replace the compiler; the 4-minute screen reproduced the 10-minute ordering.

title: Bigger-core control (width 256, no table)
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Are parameters better spent in a wider core or in tables?
settings: v0 8k, width 256, core 3.16M, total 5.3M, 600 s
data: 45 MB books corpus
results: held-out 2.003 vs 2.007 (width 128) vs 1.913 (width 128 + tables)
809 steps vs 1,277; talk-back 494 vs 732 B/s
lesson: Quadrupling the core bought nothing at equal time and answered 33% slower; tables bought 4.7% at 9% step cost.

title: Ladder 2c: seed noise and a 4-gram table
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: How large is seed noise, and does a 4-gram table add anything?
settings: 4-minute runs, seeds 1 and 2
data: 45 MB books corpus
results: v0 8k no table: 2.189 / 2.193 (0.2% spread)
v0 8k + bigram+trigram: 2.140 / 2.127 (0.6%)
+ 4-gram table (405M): 2.140
lesson: Seed noise is 0.2-0.6%; at 13M training tokens almost every 4-gram context is seen once.

title: Ladder 2d: exact n-gram output tables, first attempt (self-count bug)
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Can exact bigram/trigram follower counts mixed into the output through a trust head help the small core?
settings: 16 followers per context, 3.3M entries built in 4 s, 4-minute runs
data: 45 MB books corpus
results: n-gram output tables: 2.252 at 60 s (validation) then stall; held-out 2.140; OOD 5.20 vs 4.23 for plain words
with input tables as well: held-out 2.155, OOD 5.37
lesson: Tables counted on the training text include the current occurrence, so the trust head over-trusts rare contexts; fix was leave-one-out counting.

title: Ladder 2d second attempt: leave-one-out counting
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Does removing the current occurrence from the counts in training fix the stall?
settings: same as L2d, 4-minute runs
data: 45 MB books corpus
results: exact tables, leave-one-out: held-out 1.881, OOD 4.04, talk-back 606 B/s (1.9M learned params)
both table kinds: 1.870, OOD 4.08
plain 3-gram count model: 1.865
lesson: Leave-one-out was the whole difference: four minutes beat every ten-minute run with 1.9M learned parameters.

title: One-time side-by-side against traditional models
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: How does the best configuration compare with standard BPE and raw bytes on the same core?
settings: 0.79M-parameter Transformer, 600 s on a 4-core CPU, validation split and plateau stop (not triggered)
data: 45 MB books corpus; BPE 8,192 merges learned on the training text
results: raw bytes 2.181 (+7.6% vs BPE), BPE 8k 2.028, compiler v0 8k 2.007 (-1.0%), + hashed tables 1.913 (-5.7%), + exact tables 1.835 (-9.5%), + both 1.806 (-10.9%)
equal text (16.95 MB): n-gram models 1.676 and 1.654 vs 1.847 for BPE on validation
slower loss form found in non-n-gram models (356 vs 202 ms per step), unified afterwards
verdict: adopted as reference (not to be repeated)
lesson: The compiler alone is a wash against BPE; its value is the stable codes that make exact tables possible.

title: Scale check: 200 MB corpus, and where the gain lives
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Does the gain over BPE survive 4.4x more data, and which words carry it?
settings: 600 s, width 128; trust head with two extra confidence features (re-run at 45 MB: 1.804 vs 1.806)
data: corpus v1: 200.6 MB, 297 books; Walden added as a fourth held-out book
results: OOD at 200 MB: 3.80 vs 3.72 (hybrid behind)
by class: top-100 codes 0 gain; ranks 101-1,000 16.6%; 1,001-8,192 10.6%; byte-fallback words -8.0%
lesson: The gain lives in the middle and rare vocabulary; tables get over-confident off-domain as books grow.
sources: docs/ENCODER_RESEARCH_PLAN.md: The scale check; Where the gain lives

title: Ladder 3: four-minute screens on the hybrid (corpus v2)
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Which follower count, table size and context length to carry forward?
settings: 4-minute screens
data: corpus v2: 233 MB (v1 + 44 books from Adam's 100-book file), 48 MiB Wikipedia training split and 2 MiB Wikipedia OOD test kept separate
results: reference (hashed 2^20 + exact, 16 followers) 1.834
exact only, 16 followers 1.846
exact only, 64 followers 1.795 (best), talk-back 532 B/s
hashed 2^18 + exact 1.834
1,024-code context 1.964 (133 steps vs 622)
Wikipedia OOD about 4.5 bits/byte for every model
lesson: Keeping more of each context's followers helped 2.1%; hashed tables became nearly redundant; long context cannot be screened in 4 minutes.

title: Learning by reading: knowledge added to the tables with no retraining
phase: 3 · Encoding ladders and count tables
question: Does adding one book by an author to the count tables, with the network untouched, improve prediction of another book by her?
settings: exact tables, 64 followers, trained 240 s
data: 45 MB corpus with every Austen book removed; Pride and Prejudice (692 KB) added; control The Secret Garden
results: Emma bits/byte: 1.8199 without Austen
plus Pride and Prejudice 1.8092 (-0.59%)
plus The Secret Garden 1.8195 (-0.02%)
verdict: adopted (tables kept as a store that learns by reading)
lesson: The mechanism works (30 times the control's effect) but is small because one book is 1.6% of the counts.

title: First talking-bot test on question-and-answer text
phase: 4 · The bot that could not answer
question: Can the best configuration answer questions after training on chat-formatted instructions?
settings: 600 s from scratch, validation split; compiler + exact tables (64 followers) vs compiler alone
data: Alpaca, 52,002 exchanges, 19 MB, rendered 'User: / Assistant:'
results: held-out exchanges: tables 1.356 vs plain 1.673 bits/byte (19% better)
neither answered any of ten questions; tables gave the same opening for every question; plain model produced digit runs
lesson: Prediction and answering are different: tables keyed on the last codes are identical after 'Assistant:', so the question never reaches the output.

title: Design v2 screen 1: exchange memory keyed on the question (runs 1-3)
phase: 4 · The bot that could not answer
question: Does a question-keyed exchange memory let the model answer, and does the network learn to use it?
settings: 0.79M core (128 wide, 4 layers), ctx 256, retrieved span 110 codes, batch 16, 600 s CPU; run 2 50% self windows; run 3 3-nat retrieval bias
data: Alpaca, 51,000 exchanges in memory; groups seen/paraphrase/unseen/added
results: memory path 0.971 F1 / 99% exact on seen, 0.960 / 99% on 200 pairs added after training
network run 1: 0.12-0.13 F1 in every group; validation 1.356 -> 1.298 with the neighbour in the window
run 2 (tables off): F1 0.04-0.06 but topical
retrieved answer caps paraphrase at 0.27 F1
lesson: Memory answers what it holds instantly; a tiny network does not learn to copy from context, and the tables erase the question.

title: Design v2 screen 2: the learned copy head (runs 3b-8)
phase: 4 · The bot that could not answer
question: Does a learned copy head over the retrieved exchange carry memory into the answer?
settings: 0.79M core, ctx 256, span 110, batch 16, 600 s on the local CPU; flags --copy-head, --evidence, --fold-keys, --copy-answer-only
data: Alpaca
results: run 3b (reproduction) seen 0.132
run 4 copy head: seen 0.482 (0.610 with bias), added 0.435, paraphrase 0.233, unseen 0.160, no memory 0.129
run 7 seed 2: seen 0.617, added 0.558, 12% exact
run 5 evidence bigram 0.447 (dropped); run 6 fold keys 44 -> 55 matches but weaker (dropped)
run 8 answer-only span 0.517 / 0.446 (not adopted)
validation worse with copy head (1.30 -> 1.43)
verdict: adopted: --copy-head over the full retrieved exchange
lesson: The copy head was the missing mechanism; its gain is entirely in carrying what memory returns.

title: Local GPU set-up and CPU/GPU parity (session 1)
phase: 5 · A real GPU and the first hard truths
question: Does the RTX 3090 reproduce the CPU results?
settings: v0_8k_ng64, 1,500 steps, seed 1, --device and --max-steps added
data: 45 MB corpus rebuilt from manifests; v1 200.4 MB, v2 235.6 MB + 50.3 MB Wikipedia split; Alpaca rebuilt
results: held-out 1.8107, validation 1.8291, OOD 3.9854 bits/byte on both devices (four decimals)
GPU 5.5x faster on the 1.9M model (124.5k vs 22.5k tokens/s)
bf16 reproduces the numbers too; GPU 2x faster at 20M+ with the ragged tables
lesson: Hardware is not a variable; the GPU can run the ladder.

title: Windows CRLF changed every corpus hash
phase: 5 · A real GPU and the first hard truths
question: Why did rebuilt corpora not match their manifests on Windows?
settings: not recorded
data: not recorded
results: corpus scripts wrote CRLF through write_text, changing every book's hash and size; fixed with write_bytes
native encoder needed an absolute path
after the fix v0 52 of 53 files byte-identical; v1 149 of 150 shared files identical (GITenberg drift)
lesson: Manifests with hashes caught a silent platform difference before any result depended on it.

title: Reasoning baseline on GSM8K
phase: 5 · A real GPU and the first hard truths
question: Can the copy-head design solve grade-school word problems?
settings: 0.79M core, ctx 256, batch 16, 600 s CPU, copy head
data: GSM8K 7,473 train / 1,319 test
results: unseen 1.0% final number right (1.7% with no memory)
problems in memory 30% (stored answer copied)
digit runs with no value ('$200000000000000')
lesson: Numbers as digit runs and no checking of results were the two defects to fix.

title: Copy-head target leak in GSM8K screens 2 and 3
phase: 5 · A real GPU and the first hard truths
question: Why did validation fall to 0.57 bits/byte while seen accuracy collapsed?
settings: not recorded
data: GSM8K with the question in the copy span
results: validation 1.65 -> 0.57 bits/byte; seen-question accuracy 30% -> 7%
a position could point at itself, whose follower is the target
fix: pointer restricted to strictly earlier positions; earlier copy-head results unaffected
lesson: An implausibly good validation score was the signal of a leak.

title: GSM8K screens: copy from question, executor and answer check
phase: 5 · A real GPU and the first hard truths
question: Do copying operands from the question and an exact executor fix arithmetic?
settings: 0.79M core, 600 s CPU; --copy-question; --calculator (executor writes every 'a op b =' result, stated answer must be computed)
data: GSM8K
results: before leak fix: unseen 0% and 0%; executor replaced 201 of 203 stated answers
after fix (2b/3b): unseen 1.0% -> 1.0% -> 2.0% (2 and 4 of 198)
stored problems 33-35% final number right, F1 0.80; executor 68 confirmed, 306 replaced
lesson: Set-up of operations, not computing, is the problem; the executor cannot rescue a wrong set-up.

title: Scale run: exact-table gain against core size (session 3)
phase: 5 · A real GPU and the first hard truths
question: Does the exact-table gain over BPE hold at 4.7M and 19M?
settings: 5M: 256w x 6L, ctx 256, batch 64, 1,800 s; 20M: 448w x 8L, 2,700 s; bf16; 49M pair dropped
data: corpus v2 books + Wikipedia split (286 MB, 89.7M codes)
results: 4.7M: BPE 1.4120 vs ours 1.4115 (tie)
19M: BPE 1.3487 vs ours 1.3621 (1.0% worse; 1.8% at equal text)
code: ours better at both sizes
verdict: tables rejected as the scaling mechanism; kept as reading store
lesson: Exact counts are a crutch for a core too small to learn the statistics and a hindrance once it can (+10%, 0, -1%); memory and the copy head are the mechanism.

title: R0: bigger window (512) for the copy head

question: Was truncation of the retrieved exchange limiting the copy head?
settings: 0.8M core, window 512, span 300, 600 s CPU

title: R1d: 19M core adapted, equal time
phase: 6 · Seeds, a larger core, reading the transcripts
question: Does the floor keep rising with core size once the core knows language?
settings: 19M (448w x 8L) from the 20M scale checkpoint, 600 s GPU, 6,694 steps, greedy

title: Long-context guide review: gaps 1-8
phase: 15 · Long context: the window is not the answer
question: What did our long-context plan miss, measured against our own results?
settings: Review of a long-context training guide against the plan and results; data check of what is on disk
data: Data check: rehearsal/core text has \f document separators (446 whole books ~400k chars; wiki ~8k chars/doc; fineweb ~5k); Q&A 50,965 exchanges (answers median 185 chars); conversations 209,502, max 14 turns; no long-document QA or multi-hop set on disk
results: Gap 1: evidence only ever in a <=400-code slot at the window start (needle missed at 2,048; recall loss 0.003) -> buried-evidence windows
Gap 2: BUG chat_engine.py:206 skips the last 12 exchanges as 'in window' though only ~5 long turns fit -> recall 0/15 at 10 filler turns (15/15 at 20)
Gap 3: aux loss has no 'nothing here' target (B lost IDK -3, clarify -3) -> attention-on-SEP answerability target
Gap 4: recall windows too easy -> recall v2 (depth spread, same-attribute distractors, corrections by name, two-step, 25% absent)
Gap 5: no accuracy-by-length x depth grid -> own RULER-style grid
Gap 6: 1,024 -> 2,048 without RoPE scaling: fine to 2,048, 7.7 bits past 3.5k -> 4,096 test later
Gap 7: check rehearsal separators (checked: mostly fine)
Gap 8: story loop with state in session memory before story training
Proposed v2.1 mix: Q&A 25, skills 20, convo 15, recall v2 10, buried evidence 15, rehearsal 15
lesson: A window is only room to store text; the model must be trained to find evidence wherever it sits. Million-token windows, a teacher model and reinforcement learning stay out.

title: Session-memory bug fix (gap 2)

title: Diagnosis: why v2.3 lost ground

data: the v2.2 and v2.3 trainers and datasets
